blocks.text:
Electron Emission

➢ Emission of electron from a metal surface, when energy is incident upon the surface.

Types of Electron Emission

1. Thermionic emission

2. Field emission

3. Photoelectric emission

Work Function ($\phi$ ) : It is the minimum energy required by an electron to escape from metal surface.

Work function depends on the nature of metal and its surface.

Minimum : Cs = 2.14 eV ; Maximum : Pt = 5.65 eV

$\left(1 \mathrm{eV}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}\right)$

Einstein's Quantum theory of Light

➢ Light behaves as Quanta, when it interacts with the matter. These energy quanta are called photons, having definite Energy and Momentum.

➢ Photons always travel with speed of light in vacuum. $(c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)$

➢ Photons are electrically neutral and are not affected by electric and magnetic fields.

Photon:- Energy radiated from a source propagates (microscopically) in the form of small packets and these are known as photons.

$E \propto \nu  \Rightarrow E = h\nu $

$E = \frac{{hc}}{\lambda }(\because c = \nu \lambda ) \Rightarrow E = \frac{{hc}}{\lambda } = \frac{{12400}}{\lambda }eV - {\AA}[\because hc = 12400({\AA} - eV)]$

Here;  E = energy of photon, c = speed of light, h = Planck's constant $(h = 6.62 \times {10^{ - 34}}J - s)$

Properties of photon:-

1. Energy of photon:- Energy of a photon is directly proportional to the frequency of the radiation.

$E \propto v=h v=\frac{h c}{\lambda}=\frac{12400}{\lambda} e V-\text{\AA}
$

2. Linear momentum of photon:-

$p = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{{h\nu }}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda }$

3. Effective mass of photon:-

$\mathrm{m}=\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{c}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\mathrm{c}^2 \lambda}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{c} \mathrm{\lambda}} \quad \text { i.e. effective mass } \mathrm{m} \propto \frac{1}{\lambda}$

4. The rest mass of a photon is zero.

5. It is charge less so remains unaffected in electric and magnetic fields.

Intensity of light:-

$I=\frac{E}{A t}=\frac{n(h v)}{At}=\frac{P}{A}$            $\therefore {\text{  }}\left( {\frac{{h\nu }}{t}} \right) = P$

$n=\frac{N}{t}=\text { no. of photons per sec. }$

(i) When radiations are falling normally on a perfectly reflecting surface -

$\text { radiation force on the surface } \mathrm{F}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{p}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{Nh}}{\mathrm{t} \lambda}=\mathrm{n}\left[\frac{2 \mathrm{~h}}{\lambda}\right] \text { but } \mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{P} \lambda}{\mathrm{hc}}$

$\therefore \quad \mathrm{F}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~h}}{\lambda} \times \frac{\mathrm{P} \lambda}{\mathrm{hc}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{c}} \text { and Radiation pressure }=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{~A}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{cA}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{c}} \quad\left[\because \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{~A}}\right]$

(ii) When radiations are falling normally on a perfectly absorbing surface :

Radiation force $F = \frac{{\Delta P}}{t} = \frac{{Nh}}{{c\lambda }} \Rightarrow F = n\frac{h}{\lambda }{\text{ }}\left[ {\because n = \frac{{P\lambda }}{{hc}}} \right]$

$\mathrm{F}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{c}} \text { and Pressure }=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{~A}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{Ac}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{c}}$

(iii) Radiation pressure in case of partial reflection and partial absorption of radiation.

Diagram

Change in momentum of reflected photon $\Delta {P_1} = \frac{{2h}}{\lambda }$

Change in momentum of absorbed photon $\Delta {P_2} = \frac{h}{\lambda }$

$\therefore n  = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }}$

Number of photon reflected $n  = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }} \times r$

Number of photon absorbed $n  = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }}(1 - r)$

Force due to reflected photon

{F_r} = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }} \times r \times \frac{{2h}}{\lambda } = \frac{{2IAr}}{c}{\text{  }}\therefore \nu  = \frac{c}{\lambda }$

Force due to absorbed photon

{F_a} = \frac{{IA\lambda }}{{hc }} \times (1 - r)\frac{h}{\lambda } = \frac{{IA}}{c}{\text{(1}} - {\text{r)}}$

{F_{net}} = {F_r} + {F_a}$

{F_{net}} = \frac{{IA}}{c}(1 - r) + \frac{{2IAr}}{c} = \frac{{IA}}{c}(1 + r)$

Hence radiation pressure is

$P = \frac{{IA}}{c}(1 + r) \times \frac{1}{A}$

$P = \frac{I}{c}(1 + r)$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Incorrect Use of Constants: Using wrong values for constants like Planck's constant, speed of light, or electron charge.

    • Confusing Energy and Frequency: Misapplying the photon energy formula by confusing energy and frequency, or failing to convert between wavelength and frequency.
    • Confusing Intensity and Photon Energy: Misinterpreting light intensity as affecting photon energy, whereas intensity relates to the number of photons, not their energy.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Photoelectric Effect: It is a phenomenon of ejecting electrons by falling light of suitable frequency or suitable wavelength on a metal. Ejected electron are called photoelectrons and current flowing due to the photoelectrons is called photoelectric current. This effect was discovered by Hertz.

Experimental Setup:

Saturation current: When all the photo electrons emitted by cathode reach the anode then current flowing in the circuit at that instant is known as saturated current, this is the maximum value of photoelectric current.

Stopping potential: Minimum magnitude of negative potential of anode with respect to cathode for which current is zero is called stopping potential. This is also known as cutoff voltage. This voltage is independent of intensity.

Observations of Photoelectric Effect:

1. The effect of potential difference between A and C:

Stopping potential measures maximum kinetic energy of photo electrons. i.e. $K_{m a x}=e V_0$

2. Effect of intensity of light: When intensity of given source able to produce PEE, is increased, $\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{s}} \text { increases but } \mathrm{V}_0 \text { remains unchanged. }$

3. Effect of frequency: When frequency of radiations is increased,$V_0 \text { increases but } i_s \text { is almost unchanged. }$It is also observed that below a certain frequency photoelectrons don't come out. The minimum frequency which can eject the photo electrons is called cut off or threshold frequency. Similarly corresponding maximum wavelength is called threshold wavelength.

4.Time lag: There is no time lag between the incidence of radiations and emission of electrons. The photoelectric emission is an instantaneous process without any apparent time$\text { lag ( } \sim 10^{-9} \mathrm{~s} \text { or less), }$even when the incident radiation is made exceedingly dim.

blocks.text:
Einstein's Photoelectric Equation :- The energy of the incident light is used as energy required to release electron from a material's surface and its remaining part is acquired by the emitted electrons as their kinetic energy

$\begin{aligned} & h v=k_{\max }+\phi \\ & k_{\max }=h v-\phi \\ & V_0=\frac{h v}{e}-\frac{\phi}{e} \end{aligned}$

Explanation of PEE on basis of Einstein's Photoelectric Equation :-

1. It means maximum K.E. and stopping potential $\left(V_0\right)$ depends on frequency. It is independent of intensity of the given source.

2. Since Kinetic energy cannot be negative so that, $h \nu>\phi$ This shows the existence of threshold frequency.

$\text { Graph between (K.E. })_{\max } \text { and frequency }$

$(\mathrm{K})_{\text {max }}=\mathrm{h} v-\phi \quad[\because \quad \mathrm{Y}=\mathrm{mx}-\mathrm{c}]$

$\text { slope }=\mathrm{m}=\tan \theta=h \text { (same for all metals) }$

$\phi_B>\phi_A$

Graph between stopping potential $\left(\mathrm{V}_0\right) $ and frequency $(v)$

$\begin{aligned} &$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{eV_o}=\mathrm{h} v-\phi \\ & \mathrm{~V}_0=\left[\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{e}}\right] v-\left[\frac{\phi}{\mathrm{e}}\right] \end{aligned}$$\\ &\text { slope }=\mathrm{m}=\tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{e}} \text { (same for all metals) } \end{aligned}$$

Quantum Efficiency

$\text { Quantum efficiency }(n)=\frac{\text { number of electrons emitted per second }}{\text { total number of photons incident per second }}=\frac{n_e}{n_{p h}}$

$\text { If quantum efficiency is } n \% \text { then } n_e=\frac{n}{100} n_{p h} \quad\left[\text { Here, } n_{p h}=\left(5 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~J}^{-1} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}\right) \mathrm{P} \lambda\right]$

Photocell : A photo cell is a practical application of the phenomenon of photo electric effect, It converts light energy into electrical energy.

Failure of Wave Theory in Explanation of Photoelectric Effect:-

1. According to wave theory when light incident on a surface, energy is distributed continuously over the surface. So that electron must take a time interval to accumulate sufficient energy to come out. But in experiment there is no time lag.

2. When intensity is increased, more energetic electrons should be emitted. So that stopping potential should be intensity dependent. But it is not observed.

3. According to wave theory, if intensity is sufficient then, at each frequency, electron emission is possible. It means there should not be existence of threshold frequency.

blocks.question: Light quanta with an energy 4.9 eV eject photoelectrons from metal with work function 4.5 eV. Find the maximum impulse transmitted to the surface of the metal when each electron flies out.
blocks.answer:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation

$\mathrm{K}_{\max }=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2{ }_{\max }=\mathrm{h} v-\phi_0=4.9-4.5=0.4 \mathrm{eV}$

$\text { Change of momentum }\left(p_2-p_1\right)=\text { impulse } \therefore \text { impulse }=m v-\left(-\frac{E}{c}\right)=m v+E / c$

$\text { Maximum impulse }=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}_{\max }}+\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{c}}$

$=\sqrt{2 \times 0.4 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}}+\frac{4.9 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{3 \times 10^8}=3.43 \times 10^{-25} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

blocks.title: Core concept
blocks.text:
Moving particles of matter should display wave like properties under suitable conditions. Because nature loves symmetry and the two basic physical entities- matter and energy, must have symmetrical character. If radiation shows dual aspects, so matter should also show dual nature (particle as well as wave).

Introduction of matter waves / De-Broglie waves

1. Matter waves are associated with moving particles, not stationary ones.

2. Macroscopic objects don't exhibit wave-like properties due to their tiny wavelengths, but microscopic particles (sub-atomic) do, and their wave character is measurable.

Formula for de-Broglie wavelength:-

$\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{mv}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}}}$

De-Broglie wavelength for a charged particle-

Consider a charged particle of mass 'm' and charge 'q' accelerated from rest through a potential V, then its

$\text { (a) Kinetic energy K = qV }$

$\text { (b) Momentum } \mathrm{p}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}}$

$\text { (c) Velocity } \mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{qV}}{\mathrm{~m}}}\left[\because \mathrm{~K}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv^2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{~K}}{\mathrm{~m}}}\right]$

$\text { (d) de-Broglie wavelength } \lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}}}$

Examples of different charged particles

1. Electron:

$\text { Electron }\left({e}^–\right): \mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{e}}=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg} ; \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{e}}=\mathrm{e}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$

$\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{12.27}{\sqrt{\mathrm{~V}}} \AA \sqrt{\text { volt }}=\sqrt{\frac{150}{\mathrm{~V}}} \AA \sqrt{\text { volt }}$

2. Proton:

$\left({ }_1 p^1\right): m_p=1.67 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg} ; q_p=e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$

$\lambda_{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{0.2863}{\sqrt{\mathrm{~V}}} \AA \sqrt{\text { volt }}$

3. Deutron:

$(\text{}_{1}^{2}\text{H or d}): \text{m}_d = \text{m}_p + \text{m}_n \approx 2\text{m}_p; \quad \text{q}_d = \text{q}_p + \text{q}_n = e + 0 = e$

$\lambda_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{0.2021}{\sqrt{\mathrm{~V}}} \AA \sqrt{\text { volt }}$

4. Alpha particle:

$\left(\alpha \text { or }{ }_2 \mathrm{He}^4\right): \mathrm{m}_{\alpha}=2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}}+2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{n}} \approx 4 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}} ; \mathrm{q}_\alpha=2 \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{p}}+2 \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{n}}=2 \mathrm{e}+0=2 \mathrm{e}$

$\lambda_\alpha=\frac{0.1012}{\sqrt{\mathrm{~V}}} \AA \sqrt{\text { volt }}$

De-Broglie wavelength of Unchanged particles:

1. Neutron $\left({}_0 n^1\right):$

$\begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{ll} \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{n}}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{~K}}}    \end{array}\\  \end{aligned}$

Here K must be in joule (J)

$\\ \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{0.2863}{\sqrt{\mathrm{~K}}} \AA \sqrt{\mathrm{eV}}$

Here, K must be in eV

$$

2. Gas molecule:  Total kinetic energy of any gas molecule is $\frac{\mathrm{f}}{2} \mathrm{kT} \text { where };\mathrm{f}=\text { degree of freedom. }$But total translatory kinetic energy of any gas molecule is$\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{kT}$Because de-Broglie wavelength is associated with translational motion only. Therefore, for any gas molecule

$\begin{aligned} &\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{kT}\right)}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{3 \mathrm{mkT}}}\\ &\text { (Here } \mathrm{T} \text { is in kelvin) } \end{aligned}$

blocks.text:
Nucleus:

(1) Central core of every atom.

(2)Discovered by Rutherford in $\alpha$ -scattering experiment.

(3)The order of nucleus size $=10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}$ or fm while the order of atomic size = $10^{-10} \mathrm{~m} \text { or } \AA$

(4)Protons and neutrons, together referred as nucleons.

(5) A nuclide is represented by { }_Z^A \mathrm{X}$

$\mathrm{Z}=\text { atomic number = } \mathrm{p} \text { (no. of protons) }$

$\mathrm{A}=\text { mass number }=\text { total no. of nucleons }=\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{p}$

Atomic masses are generally represented by atomic mass unit (u)

$1 \mathrm{u}=\frac{\text { mass of } \mathrm{C}^{12} \text { atom }}{12}=1.66 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}$

Types of Nuclei:

(1) Isotope: same Z

(2) Isobar: same A

(3) Isotone: same (A – Z)

Properties of Nuclei:

As the number of nucleons in nucleus increases its size also increases and relation between its radius and mass number is

$\mathrm{R} \propto \mathrm{~A}^{1 / 3} \rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{R}_0 \mathrm{~A}^{1 / 3}$

$\text { Here } R_0 \text { is a constant and its value } R_0 \approx 1.2 \mathrm{fm} \text {. }$

Volume of Nucleus: $\text { Volume } \propto R^3\left(B u t R \propto A^{1 / 3}\right) \quad \text { or } \quad \text { volume } \propto A$

Density of Nucleus ($ \rho $):

$\rho=\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { volume }} \cong \frac{A m_p}{\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3}=\frac{A m_p}{\frac{4}{3} \pi R_0{ }^3 A}=\frac{3 m_p}{4 \pi R_0^3}=2.3 \times 10^{17} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$

It means $ \rho$ is independent of A . Density of nuclei of all types of element is same and its order is

$10^{17} \,\text{kg/m}^3$$\text { or } 10^{14} \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^3$.

Features of Nuclear Force $\left(F_n\right)$:

1. The strongest force in the universe.

2. Works only between the nucleons.

3. Very short range : only upto size of nucleus (3 or 4 fermi). More than this distance, nuclear force is almost zero.

4. Very much depends upon distance :– Small variation in distance may cause of large change in nuclear force while electrostatic force remains almost unaffected.

5. Independent of charge :– Interacts between n–n as well as between p–p and also between n–p.

6. Spin dependent :– It is stronger between nucleons having same sense of spin than between nucleons having opposite sense of spin.

7. It is not a central force Electrostatic and gravitational forces are central forces.

8.Nature: – (A) Attractive – If distance is greater than 0.8 fm or above.

(B) Repulsive – If distance is lesser than 0.8 fm.

Einstein's Mass - Energy Relation:-According to Einstein, mass can be converted into energy and energy into mass. This relation is given by $E=m c^2$

$E=\text { total energy associated with mass } m \text { }$

$c^2 \text { is used as a conversion coefficient }$

Mass defect: Mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of masses of its constituent nucleons. This difference is called mass defect.

(1) If observed mass of nucleus { }_Z X^A $ be $\text{M}$, mass of proton is $M_p$ and mass of neutron is $M_n $, then

mass defect = $\Delta \mathrm{m}=\left[\mathrm{ZM}_{\mathrm{p}}+(\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{Z}) \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{n}}\right]-\mathrm{M}$

(2) If  M  is taken as mass atom of {}^{A}_{Z}X$ instead of mass of nucleus then$$

$\Delta \mathrm{m}=\left[\mathrm{Z}\left(\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{p}}+\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{e}}\right)+(\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{Z}) \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{n}}\right]-\mathrm{M}_{\text {atom }}$

Binding energy  $\left(E_b\right)$: Binding energy of a nucleus is the energy required to split it into its nucleons (free).

$\Delta \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{b}}=\Delta \mathrm{m} \cdot \mathrm{c}^2$

It is always positive and numerically equal to the energy equivalent of mass defect (or equal to the energy liberated when it was formed)

$\text { Binding energy per nucleus }=\frac{B . E .}{\text { mass number }}=\frac{B . E .}{A}$

$\text { Stability } \propto \frac{\text { B.E. }}{\text { A }}$

Binding Energy per Nucleon Curve:

(1) The value of binding energy per nucleon decides the stability of a nucleus. It is obtained by dividing binding energy by the mass number of given nucleus.

(2) The following figure shows the binding energy per nucleon plotted against the mass number of various atoms nuclei. Greater the binding energy per nucleon, the more stable the nucleus.

(3) It is maximum for isotope of iron-{ }_{26}^{56} \mathrm{Fe} \text { and is } 8.8 \mathrm{MeV} / \text { nucleon. }$It is the most stable nucleus.

(4) For Uranium, binding energy per nucleon is about 7.7 MeV/nucleon and it is unstable.

(5) The medium size nuclei are more stable than light or heavy nuclei.

Dalton's Atomic Theory: Atoms are indivisible. It  cannot be subdivided. If can neither be created nor be distroyed.

Thomson's Atom Model:

1. An atom is electrically neutral because the positive charge is equal to the negative charge of electrons.

2.The positive charge and the whole mass of the atom is uniformly distributed throughout the sphere in which electrons are embedded in between.

Shortcomings of Thomson's model:

(1) Could not explain spectrum of atoms

(2) Could not explain Scattering of –$\alpha$ particles

Rutherford atomic model:

1. Most alpha particles pass through the atom without deflection, indicating the atom is mostly empty space.

2. A few alpha particles are deflected at large angles or even bounce back, suggesting the presence of a dense, positively charged nucleus.

3. The nucleus contains most of the atom's mass and all of its positive charge.

4. Electrons, being very light, do not significantly affect the path of alpha particles.

Nearer distance of approach:

$\mathrm{r}_0=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \times \frac{2 \mathrm{Ze}^2}{\left[\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}_0^2\right]}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \frac{2 \mathrm{Ze}^2}{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{K}}} \quad \text { (Where, } \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{K}}=\text { K.E. of } \alpha-\text { Particle) }$

Failure of Rutherford's Atomic model:

(1) It could not explain the stability of atom.

(2) It could not explain the discrete nature of hydrogen spectra.

Assumptions of Bohr Model:

(1) Electron revolves circular orbit around nucleus

(2) Electron is allowed to be present in certain fixed orbits only whose angular momentum is

$\mathrm{mvr}=\frac{\mathrm{nh}}{2 \pi}$.These are called stationary energy levels or shells.

(3) Electrons denote radiate energy when in shells but energy is radiated or absorbed  when an electron jumps to lower or higher orbit respectively.

$\mathrm{E}_2-\mathrm{E}_1=\mathrm{h} v$

Drawbacks of Bohr Model:

  • This model could not explain the fine structure of spectral lines, Zeeman and Stark effect.
  • This model is valid only for single electron systems.
  • This model is based on circular orbits of electrons whereas in reality there is no orbit.
  • This model could not explain the intensity of spectral lines.
  • It could not explain the doublets obtained in the spectra of some of the atoms.
  • Bohr's model is semi quantum model, it means, it includes two quantum numbers (E and L)  but unfortunately it considers circular motion of electron.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Electron Emission

➢ Emission of electron from a metal surface, when energy is incident upon the surface.

Types of Electron Emission

1. Thermionic emission

2. Field emission

3. Photoelectric emission

Work Function ($\phi$ ) : It is the minimum energy required by an electron to escape from metal surface.

Work function depends on the nature of metal and its surface.

Minimum : Cs = 2.14 eV ; Maximum : Pt = 5.65 eV

$\left(1 \mathrm{eV}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}\right)$

Einstein's Quantum theory of Light

➢ Light behaves as Quanta, when it interacts with the matter. These energy quanta are called photons, having definite Energy and Momentum.

➢ Photons always travel with speed of light in vacuum. $(c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)$

➢ Photons are electrically neutral and are not affected by electric and magnetic fields.

Photon:- Energy radiated from a source propagates (microscopically) in the form of small packets and these are known as photons.

$E \propto \nu  \Rightarrow E = h\nu $

$E = \frac{{hc}}{\lambda }(\because c = \nu \lambda ) \Rightarrow E = \frac{{hc}}{\lambda } = \frac{{12400}}{\lambda }eV - {\AA}[\because hc = 12400({\AA} - eV)]$

Here;  E = energy of photon, c = speed of light, h = Planck's constant $(h = 6.62 \times {10^{ - 34}}J - s)$

Properties of photon:-

1. Energy of photon:- Energy of a photon is directly proportional to the frequency of the radiation.

$E \propto v=h v=\frac{h c}{\lambda}=\frac{12400}{\lambda} e V-\text{\AA}
$

2. Linear momentum of photon:-

$p = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{{h\nu }}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda }$

3. Effective mass of photon:-

$\mathrm{m}=\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{c}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\mathrm{c}^2 \lambda}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{c} \mathrm{\lambda}} \quad \text { i.e. effective mass } \mathrm{m} \propto \frac{1}{\lambda}$

4. The rest mass of a photon is zero.

5. It is charge less so remains unaffected in electric and magnetic fields.

Intensity of light:-

$I=\frac{E}{A t}=\frac{n(h v)}{At}=\frac{P}{A}$            $\therefore {\text{  }}\left( {\frac{{h\nu }}{t}} \right) = P$

$n=\frac{N}{t}=\text { no. of photons per sec. }$

(i) When radiations are falling normally on a perfectly reflecting surface -

$\text { radiation force on the surface } \mathrm{F}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{p}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{Nh}}{\mathrm{t} \lambda}=\mathrm{n}\left[\frac{2 \mathrm{~h}}{\lambda}\right] \text { but } \mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{P} \lambda}{\mathrm{hc}}$

$\therefore \quad \mathrm{F}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~h}}{\lambda} \times \frac{\mathrm{P} \lambda}{\mathrm{hc}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{c}} \text { and Radiation pressure }=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{~A}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{cA}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{c}} \quad\left[\because \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{~A}}\right]$

(ii) When radiations are falling normally on a perfectly absorbing surface :

Radiation force $F = \frac{{\Delta P}}{t} = \frac{{Nh}}{{c\lambda }} \Rightarrow F = n\frac{h}{\lambda }{\text{ }}\left[ {\because n = \frac{{P\lambda }}{{hc}}} \right]$

$\mathrm{F}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{c}} \text { and Pressure }=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{~A}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{Ac}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{c}}$

(iii) Radiation pressure in case of partial reflection and partial absorption of radiation.

Diagram

Change in momentum of reflected photon $\Delta {P_1} = \frac{{2h}}{\lambda }$

Change in momentum of absorbed photon $\Delta {P_2} = \frac{h}{\lambda }$

$\therefore n  = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }}$

Number of photon reflected $n  = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }} \times r$

Number of photon absorbed $n  = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }}(1 - r)$

Force due to reflected photon

{F_r} = \frac{{IA}}{{h\nu }} \times r \times \frac{{2h}}{\lambda } = \frac{{2IAr}}{c}{\text{  }}\therefore \nu  = \frac{c}{\lambda }$

Force due to absorbed photon

{F_a} = \frac{{IA\lambda }}{{hc }} \times (1 - r)\frac{h}{\lambda } = \frac{{IA}}{c}{\text{(1}} - {\text{r)}}$

{F_{net}} = {F_r} + {F_a}$

{F_{net}} = \frac{{IA}}{c}(1 - r) + \frac{{2IAr}}{c} = \frac{{IA}}{c}(1 + r)$

Hence radiation pressure is

$P = \frac{{IA}}{c}(1 + r) \times \frac{1}{A}$

$P = \frac{I}{c}(1 + r)$

Einstein's Photoelectric Equation :- The energy of the incident light is used as energy required to release electron from a material's surface and its remaining part is acquired by the emitted electrons as their kinetic energy

Explanation of PEE on basis of Einstein's Photoelectric Equation :-

1. It means maximum K.E. and stopping potential $\left(V_0\right)$ depends on frequency. It is independent of intensity of the given source.

2. Since Kinetic energy cannot be negative so that, $h \nu>\phi$ This shows the existence of threshold frequency.

$\text { Graph between (K.E. })_{\max } \text { and frequency }$

$(\mathrm{K})_{\text {max }}=\mathrm{h} v-\phi \quad[\because \quad \mathrm{Y}=\mathrm{mx}-\mathrm{c}]$

$\text { slope }=\mathrm{m}=\tan \theta=h \text { (same for all metals) }$

$\phi_B>\phi_A$

Graph between stopping potential $\left(\mathrm{V}_0\right) $ and frequency $(v)$

Quantum Efficiency

$\text { Quantum efficiency }(n)=\frac{\text { number of electrons emitted per second }}{\text { total number of photons incident per second }}=\frac{n_e}{n_{p h}}$

$\text { If quantum efficiency is } n \% \text { then } n_e=\frac{n}{100} n_{p h} \quad\left[\text { Here, } n_{p h}=\left(5 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~J}^{-1} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}\right) \mathrm{P} \lambda\right]$

Photocell : A photo cell is a practical application of the phenomenon of photo electric effect, It converts light energy into electrical energy.

Failure of Wave Theory in Explanation of Photoelectric Effect:-

1. According to wave theory when light incident on a surface, energy is distributed continuously over the surface. So that electron must take a time interval to accumulate sufficient energy to come out. But in experiment there is no time lag.

2. When intensity is increased, more energetic electrons should be emitted. So that stopping potential should be intensity dependent. But it is not observed.

3. According to wave theory, if intensity is sufficient then, at each frequency, electron emission is possible. It means there should not be existence of threshold frequency.

blocks.title: Core concept
blocks.text:
Moving particles of matter should display wave like properties under suitable conditions. Because nature loves symmetry and the two basic physical entities- matter and energy, must have symmetrical character. If radiation shows dual aspects, so matter should also show dual nature (particle as well as wave).

Introduction of matter waves / De-Broglie waves

1. Matter waves are associated with moving particles, not stationary ones.

2. Macroscopic objects don't exhibit wave-like properties due to their tiny wavelengths, but microscopic particles (sub-atomic) do, and their wave character is measurable.

Formula for de-Broglie wavelength:-

$\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{mv}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}}}$

De-Broglie wavelength for a charged particle-

Consider a charged particle of mass 'm' and charge 'q' accelerated from rest through a potential V, then its

$\text { (a) Kinetic energy K = qV }$

$\text { (b) Momentum } \mathrm{p}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}}$

$\text { (c) Velocity } \mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{qV}}{\mathrm{~m}}}\left[\because \mathrm{~K}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv^2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{~K}}{\mathrm{~m}}}\right]$

$\text { (d) de-Broglie wavelength } \lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}}}$

blocks.text:
Nucleus:

(1) Central core of every atom.

(2)Discovered by Rutherford in $\alpha$ -scattering experiment.

(3)The order of nucleus size $=10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}$ or fm while the order of atomic size = $10^{-10} \mathrm{~m} \text { or } \AA$

(4)Protons and neutrons, together referred as nucleons.

(5) A nuclide is represented by { }_Z^A \mathrm{X}$

$\mathrm{Z}=\text { atomic number = } \mathrm{p} \text { (no. of protons) }$

$\mathrm{A}=\text { mass number }=\text { total no. of nucleons }=\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{p}$

Atomic masses are generally represented by atomic mass unit (u)

$1 \mathrm{u}=\frac{\text { mass of } \mathrm{C}^{12} \text { atom }}{12}=1.66 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}$

Types of Nuclei:

(1) Isotope: same Z

(2) Isobar: same A

(3) Isotone: same (A – Z)

Properties of Nuclei:

As the number of nucleons in nucleus increases its size also increases and relation between its radius and mass number is

$\mathrm{R} \propto \mathrm{~A}^{1 / 3} \rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{R}_0 \mathrm{~A}^{1 / 3}$

$\text { Here } R_0 \text { is a constant and its value } R_0 \approx 1.2 \mathrm{fm} \text {. }$

Volume of Nucleus: $\text { Volume } \propto R^3\left(B u t R \propto A^{1 / 3}\right) \quad \text { or } \quad \text { volume } \propto A$

Density of Nucleus ($ \rho $):

$\rho=\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { volume }} \cong \frac{A m_p}{\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3}=\frac{A m_p}{\frac{4}{3} \pi R_0{ }^3 A}=\frac{3 m_p}{4 \pi R_0^3}=2.3 \times 10^{17} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$

It means $ \rho$ is independent of A . Density of nuclei of all types of element is same and its order is

$10^{17} \,\text{kg/m}^3$$\text { or } 10^{14} \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^3$.

Features of Nuclear Force $\left(F_n\right)$:

1. The strongest force in the universe.

2. Works only between the nucleons.

3. Very short range : only upto size of nucleus (3 or 4 fermi). More than this distance, nuclear force is almost zero.

4. Very much depends upon distance :– Small variation in distance may cause of large change in nuclear force while electrostatic force remains almost unaffected.

5. Independent of charge :– Interacts between n–n as well as between p–p and also between n–p.

6. Spin dependent :– It is stronger between nucleons having same sense of spin than between nucleons having opposite sense of spin.

7. It is not a central force Electrostatic and gravitational forces are central forces.

8.Nature: – (A) Attractive – If distance is greater than 0.8 fm or above.

(B) Repulsive – If distance is lesser than 0.8 fm.

Einstein's Mass - Energy Relation:-According to Einstein, mass can be converted into energy and energy into mass. This relation is given by $E=m c^2$

$E=\text { total energy associated with mass } m \text { }$

$c^2 \text { is used as a conversion coefficient }$

Mass defect: Mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of masses of its constituent nucleons. This difference is called mass defect.

(1) If observed mass of nucleus { }_Z X^A $ be $\text{M}$, mass of proton is $M_p$ and mass of neutron is $M_n $, then

mass defect = $\Delta \mathrm{m}=\left[\mathrm{ZM}_{\mathrm{p}}+(\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{Z}) \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{n}}\right]-\mathrm{M}$

(2) If  M  is taken as mass atom of {}^{A}_{Z}X$ instead of mass of nucleus then$$

$\Delta \mathrm{m}=\left[\mathrm{Z}\left(\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{p}}+\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{e}}\right)+(\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{Z}) \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{n}}\right]-\mathrm{M}_{\text {atom }}$

Binding energy  $\left(E_b\right)$: Binding energy of a nucleus is the energy required to split it into its nucleons (free).

$\Delta \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{b}}=\Delta \mathrm{m} \cdot \mathrm{c}^2$

It is always positive and numerically equal to the energy equivalent of mass defect (or equal to the energy liberated when it was formed)

$\text { Binding energy per nucleus }=\frac{B . E .}{\text { mass number }}=\frac{B . E .}{A}$

$\text { Stability } \propto \frac{\text { B.E. }}{\text { A }}$

Binding Energy per Nucleon Curve:

(1) The value of binding energy per nucleon decides the stability of a nucleus. It is obtained by dividing binding energy by the mass number of given nucleus.

(2) The following figure shows the binding energy per nucleon plotted against the mass number of various atoms nuclei. Greater the binding energy per nucleon, the more stable the nucleus.

(3) It is maximum for isotope of iron-{ }_{26}^{56} \mathrm{Fe} \text { and is } 8.8 \mathrm{MeV} / \text { nucleon. }$It is the most stable nucleus.

(4) For Uranium, binding energy per nucleon is about 7.7 MeV/nucleon and it is unstable.

(5) The medium size nuclei are more stable than light or heavy nuclei.

Dalton's Atomic Theory: Atoms are indivisible. It  cannot be subdivided. If can neither be created nor be distroyed.

Thomson's Atom Model:

1. An atom is electrically neutral because the positive charge is equal to the negative charge of electrons.

2.The positive charge and the whole mass of the atom is uniformly distributed throughout the sphere in which electrons are embedded in between.

Shortcomings of Thomson's model:

(1) Could not explain spectrum of atoms

(2) Could not explain Scattering of –$\alpha$ particles

Rutherford atomic model:

1. Most alpha particles pass through the atom without deflection, indicating the atom is mostly empty space.

2. A few alpha particles are deflected at large angles or even bounce back, suggesting the presence of a dense, positively charged nucleus.

3. The nucleus contains most of the atom's mass and all of its positive charge.

4. Electrons, being very light, do not significantly affect the path of alpha particles.

Nearer distance of approach:

$\mathrm{r}_0=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \times \frac{2 \mathrm{Ze}^2}{\left[\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}_0^2\right]}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \frac{2 \mathrm{Ze}^2}{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{K}}} \quad \text { (Where, } \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{K}}=\text { K.E. of } \alpha-\text { Particle) }$

Failure of Rutherford's Atomic model:

(1) It could not explain the stability of atom.

(2) It could not explain the discrete nature of hydrogen spectra.

Assumptions of Bohr Model:

(1) Electron revolves circular orbit around nucleus

(2) Electron is allowed to be present in certain fixed orbits only whose angular momentum is

$\mathrm{mvr}=\frac{\mathrm{nh}}{2 \pi}$.These are called stationary energy levels or shells.

(3) Electrons denote radiate energy when in shells but energy is radiated or absorbed  when an electron jumps to lower or higher orbit respectively.

$\mathrm{E}_2-\mathrm{E}_1=\mathrm{h} v$

Drawbacks of Bohr Model:

  • This model could not explain the fine structure of spectral lines, Zeeman and Stark effect.
  • This model is valid only for single electron systems.
  • This model is based on circular orbits of electrons whereas in reality there is no orbit.
  • This model could not explain the intensity of spectral lines.
  • It could not explain the doublets obtained in the spectra of some of the atoms.
  • Bohr's model is semi quantum model, it means, it includes two quantum numbers (E and L)  but unfortunately it considers circular motion of electron.
